learn.hook: Some numbers can be written as a neat fraction. Others, like √2, refuse to be caught by any fraction at all, no matter how hard you try!
points: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Examples: 3 = 3/1, −0.5 = −1/2, 0 = 0/1.
Every natural number, whole number and integer is also a rational number.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q. Examples: √2, √3, √5 and π.
If n is a natural number that is not a perfect square, then √n is irrational. But √16 = 4 is rational.
Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more rational numbers; their average is always one of them.

example.q: Find three rational numbers between 1/3 and 1/2.
steps: Multiply top and bottom by 2 to make room: 8/24 and 12/24

learn.reallife: The diagonal of a square tile of side 1 m is √2 m long. A carpenter can measure it closely, but never as an exact fraction!

games.title: True or false?
items: Every integer is a rational number
Any integer n can be written as n/1.
22/7 is only a handy approximation. π is irrational, so no fraction equals it exactly.
The square root of every natural number is irrational
√9 = 3 and √25 = 5 are rational. Only non-perfect squares give irrational roots.
0 = 0/1, which is in the form p/q with q ≠ 0.
The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational
A non-zero rational number times an irrational number is always irrational.

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is irrational?
quiz.explain: 11 is not a perfect square, so √11 cannot be written as p/q. √25 = 5, 0.6 = 3/5 and −7/3 are all rational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every number with a root sign is irrational

quiz.q: Which of these numbers is rational?
quiz.explain: √36 = 6 = 6/1, which is rational. The others cannot be written as fractions.
quiz.mistake: Sees the root sign and assumes the number must be irrational

quiz.q: Which number lies between 2/5 and 3/5?
quiz.explain: 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/5 = 0.6. Their average is 1/2 = 0.5, which lies between them.
quiz.mistake: Compares only numerators or denominators instead of the whole fractions

quiz.q: Meena's calculator shows √2 = 1.414213562. Which statement is correct?
options: The display is only an approximation; √2 is irrational and its decimals never end or repeat
√2 is rational because the calculator shows a decimal
quiz.explain: √2 is irrational. A calculator can only show a few digits, so what you see is a rounded value.
quiz.mistake: Believes a calculator display is always exact

quiz.q: What kind of number is 2 + √3?
quiz.explain: A rational number plus an irrational number is always irrational. If 2 + √3 were p/q, then √3 would be p/q − 2, a fraction, which is impossible.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a whole number makes the result rational

quiz.q: What is √2 × √8?
quiz.explain: √2 × √8 = √(2 × 8) = √16 = 4. Two irrational numbers can multiply to give a rational one.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers under the root instead of multiplying them

quiz.q: How many rational numbers lie between 1 and 2?
quiz.explain: You can always find another rational number between any two, for example 1.5, 1.25, 1.125, ... so the list never ends.
quiz.mistake: Counts only decimals with one decimal place (1.1 to 1.9)

quiz.q: Which of these is a rational number even though it has a root sign?
quiz.explain: √(9/16) = √9 / √16 = 3/4, which is rational.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every square root is irrational

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: "What is the difference between a rational and an irrational number? They both look like numbers to me!"
teach.praise: So a rational number can be written as a fraction p/q, and an irrational one like √2 or π never can. Clear as a blue sky!
teach.nudge: Can every number be written as a fraction? Can you give me an example that cannot?

learn.hook: √2 is not a fraction, yet you can mark it exactly on a number line with just a ruler and a compass. Here is the trick!
points: Rational and irrational numbers together make up the real numbers.
Every real number is a point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number. The line has no gaps.
To mark √2: draw a right triangle on the line with legs 1 and 1. Its hypotenuse is √(1 + 1) = √2; swing an arc from 0 with that length.
In the same way, legs 2 and 1 give √5, and legs √2 and 1 give √3.
To compare roots, compare squares: √10 < 3.2 because 10 < 3.2² = 10.24.

example.q: Show how to mark √5 on the number line.
steps: Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line
At A, draw AB = 1 unit perpendicular to the line
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc to cut the line at P. Then OP = √5 ≈ 2.24
example.answer: P is the point √5, a little to the right of 2.2

learn.reallife: A ruler with marks only at whole and half centimetres still contains the point √2 cm: every length you can draw is a real number.

quiz.q: Between which two whole numbers does √20 lie?
quiz.explain: 4² = 16 and 5² = 25. Since 16 < 20 < 25, √20 lies between 4 and 5.
quiz.mistake: Looks at numbers near 20 instead of the squares near 20

quiz.q: To mark √2 on the number line, which right triangle do you draw?
quiz.explain: With legs 1 and 1 the hypotenuse is √(1² + 1²) = √2.
quiz.mistake: Uses legs 1 and 2, which give √5 instead

quiz.q: Which is greater, √10 or 3.2?
quiz.explain: Compare squares: (√10)² = 10 and 3.2² = 10.24. Since 10 < 10.24, 3.2 is greater.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number with a root sign must be bigger, or guesses √10 ≈ 3.3

quiz.q: From 0 on a number line, Arjun marks 3 units, draws a 2-unit perpendicular there and swings the hypotenuse down onto the line. Which number does he get?
quiz.explain: The hypotenuse is √(3² + 2²) = √(9 + 4) = √13.
quiz.mistake: Adds the legs (5) or forgets to take the square root (13)

quiz.q: Which statement about the number line is true?
options: Only rational numbers can be marked on it
√2 cannot be shown on it because its decimals never end
Every point on it stands for a real number
There are gaps that no number fills
quiz.explain: The real numbers fill the whole line: each point is a real number and each real number has a point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a number must have a finite decimal to have a place on the line

quiz.q: Which list is in increasing order?
quiz.mistake: Thinks √2 is bigger than 1.5

quiz.q: Riya jumps √9 units and then √16 more units to the right of 0. Where does she land?
quiz.explain: √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, so she lands at 3 + 4 = 7. Note that √9 + √16 is not the same as √(9 + 16) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Writes √9 + √16 = √25 = 5, adding under one root

quiz.q: √50 is closest to which value?
quiz.explain: 7² = 49, so √50 is just a little more than 7. In fact 7.07² ≈ 49.98.
quiz.mistake: Halves the number instead of taking its square root

teach.ask: Gappu holds a compass: "How can I put √2 on a number line if I can't even write it as a fraction?"
teach.praise: A right triangle with sides 1 and 1, then swing the hypotenuse down with a compass. √2 has a home on the line!
teach.nudge: What shape do I draw first, and how do I bring its long side down onto the line?

learn.hook: Divide 1 by 8 and the division stops. Divide 1 by 7 and the digits 142857 go round and round forever. Why?
points: The decimal expansion of a rational number either terminates (ends), like 3/8 = 0.375, or is non-terminating and recurring (repeats), like 1/3 = 0.333...
A fraction in lowest terms terminates only if its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5. So 7/20 terminates, but 5/12 repeats.
An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring: it never ends and never settles into a repeating block.
A repeating decimal can be turned back into p/q. For 0.777..., let x = 0.777...; then 10x = 7.777..., so 9x = 7 and x = 7/9.
The repeating block is shown with a bar on top, for example 0.27 with a bar on 27 means 0.272727...

example.q: Write 0.474747... (47 repeating) in the form p/q.
steps: Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100: 100x = 47.474747...

learn.reallife: When ₹100 is shared equally among 3 friends, each share is ₹33.333..., so in real life we round it to ₹33.33.

items.q: 0.454545... (45 repeating) as a fraction in lowest terms

quiz.q: What is the decimal expansion of 7/8?
quiz.explain: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. The division ends because 8 = 2³ has only the prime factor 2.
quiz.mistake: Just writes the numerator and denominator side by side after the point

quiz.q: Which fraction has a terminating decimal expansion?
quiz.explain: 40 = 2³ × 5 has only 2s and 5s, so 11/40 = 0.275 terminates. 7, 12 = 2² × 3 and 9 = 3² all contain other primes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an even denominator always gives a terminating decimal

quiz.q: The decimal expansion of an irrational number is:
quiz.explain: If the decimal ended or repeated, the number could be written as p/q and would be rational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any decimal that goes on forever is irrational, even if it repeats

quiz.q: Write 0.777... (7 repeating) as a fraction.
quiz.explain: Let x = 0.777...; 10x = 7.777...; subtracting gives 9x = 7, so x = 7/9.
quiz.mistake: Writes 7/10, treating the repeating decimal as if it stopped after one digit

quiz.q: Write 0.363636... (36 repeating) in lowest terms.
quiz.explain: Two digits repeat: 100x − x = 36, so x = 36/99 = 4/11.
quiz.mistake: Uses 90 instead of 99 when two digits repeat

quiz.q: 1/7 = 0.142857142857... How many digits are in its repeating block?
quiz.explain: The block 142857 repeats, and it has 6 digits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the block length must equal the denominator 7

quiz.q: Aisha shares ₹100 equally among 3 friends. Which describes 100/3 as a decimal?
quiz.explain: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.333..., with 3 repeating forever. It repeats, so it is rational, not irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rounded money value is the exact answer

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.explain: In 0.1211211121111... the number of 1s keeps growing, so no fixed block repeats. It never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long decimal is irrational without checking for a repeating block

teach.ask: Gappu taps the calculator: "Some decimals stop, some repeat and some go wild. How can I tell which numbers are rational from their decimals?"
teach.praise: Decimals that end or repeat belong to rational numbers; decimals that never end and never repeat are irrational. Tweet-tastic!
teach.nudge: What happens to the decimal of 1/3 compared with √2? Does one of them repeat?
